https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y0.text: Image source, Getty Images By Olivia Ireland Â and Â Sareen Habeshian Published 43 minutes ago Harvard has agreed to pay $53 million (Â£39 million) to resolve lawsuits from families who alleged the university mishandled the bodies of loved ones donated to its medical school. The settlement, proposed in a Boston court on Monday, would end the suits filed against Harvard âMedical School (HMS) after former morgue manager Cedric Lodge pleaded guilty to stealing and selling human remains on the black market. Lodge, 58, took parts from cadavers and sold them online in a scheme that allegedly ran from 2018 to 2021. The medical school said in a letter it shared on Monday that multi-million dollar settlement funds will be set up for families once the court grants approval. Lodge and six other co-conspirators who had no connection to Harvard were all indicted and pleaded guilty in 2025. Prosecutors have alleged Lodge used his position as the manager of the "Anatomical Gifts Program" at the medical school to dismember cadavers donated for medical research. Harvard students use donated bodies to study and practice medical procedures. When the school finishes using them, the cadavers are often cremated and remains returned to their families, or buried in the university's medical cemetery, according to the indictment . Lodge and his wife sold the body parts to buyers in Pennsylvania and Massachusetts, the indictment states. He was sentenced in December to eight years in prison, according to the Department of Justice. His wife was sentenced to one year and a day. In 2023, a number of civil lawsuits were brought against Harvard alleging the university ignored Lodge's misconduct for several years until he was indicted. While the cases were initially dismissed by a state court judge, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court revived the suits last fall. On Monday, both Harvard and the plaintiffs in those cases asked the court to approve the class-action settlement agreement valued at $53 million. The university's letter - signed by George Daley, â Harvard's dean of the faculty of medicine, and Bernard Chang, the dean for medical education at Harvard Medical School - said: "Lodge's criminal acts were morally reprehensible and inconsistent with the standards that Harvard University and HMS expect for the treatment of anatomical donors and their loved ones". Starting in the 2027-2028 academic year, the medical school will also establish an annual financial-aid scholarship for medical students "in appreciation and in honour of all of our anatomical donors," the letter states. It adds that while Lodge's sentencing and the settlement conclude the case, "the process of recovering from this painful incident continues". https://www.politico.eu/article/nato-nex.text: BRUSSELS — NATO is bracing for the very real possibility that the next French president could tear a gaping hole in the alliance. As the alliance grapples with doubts over Washington’s defense commitment to Europe and rearms to prepare for a possible attack by Russia, recent French polling shows around half of French voters in next year's election are backing hardline candidates who have objections to NATO. Marine Le Pen from the far-right National Rally party wants to pull Paris out of the bloc’s integrated command, while Jean-Luc Mélechon on the far left has said he wants to quit the alliance. Advertisement Advertisement A pullback from NATO by France — the EU’s only nuclear power — would send shockwaves through the alliance, throwing French deployments in Romania and Estonia into doubt, curbing access to key battlefield kit and blunting military coordination among the 32 members. And the timing could also not be worse. Under Donald Trump, the U.S. has begun scaling back forces in Europe, leaving other allies racing to build up their defenses in response to warnings that Russia could attack the alliance this decade . “With a lesser U.S. presence, what you don't want is a major European country distancing itself from the alliance, particularly at a time where the whole goal is for the Europeans, including France of course, to take on more responsibility,” said Jamie Shea, a senior defense fellow at the Friends of Europe think tank and a former NATO spokesperson. The repercussions of leaving NATO’s unified command would spell trouble for Paris as well as the alliance. “We hope that France understands the long-term benefits of a strong NATO … and that [requires] also France to be integrated quite fully in NATO structures,” Finnish Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen told POLITICO. “So we hope that in defense policy … they will keep their political line in a strong position.” With the presidential elections still eight months out, the outcome is far from certain. There’s also a chance candidates could soften their views on the alliance once elected — much like Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni did in 2022. But given the country’s historically fraught relationship with the alliance, the threat to NATO is a serious one. Advertisement Advertisement “I fear those elections,” said one NATO diplomat, who like others for this story was granted anonymity to speak freely about the sensitive matter. “Losing France would be dreadful.” Plus ça change ... This wouldn’t be the first time France left NATO’s integrated command. In 1966, then-French President Charles De Gaulle ended his country's participation in NATO military structures, citing a need for greater sovereignty. He booted out around 26,000 troops and forced NATO’s relocation to Belgium. Paris only reversed that decision in 2009, under former President Nicolas Sarkozy. Nicolas Sarkozy departs after addressing the General Assembly of the United Nations in New York in September 2009. | Jeff Zelevansky/Getty Images If it happens again, Paris is unlikely to fully cut ties with the alliance, said Fabrice Pothier, CEO of the Rasmussen Global political consultancy and NATO’s former head of policy planning. However, “it would be foolish to think that there would be continuity” under a new hard-line president, he said. “The French have never been the most pro-NATO members,” he said, making the issue “low-hanging fruit” for populists. According to internal alliance polling from this spring, which was seen by POLITICO, some 54 percent of French voters said they would vote to stay in NATO — the second-lowest of NATO’s 32 members after Montenegro. Advertisement Advertisement And while France’s two-round presidential election system has previously prevented hardliners from winning as voters rally around more moderate candidates, that may not happen next year. Both Le Pen and Mélenchon have made their cases loud and clear. “We must leave NATO’s integrated command,” Le Pen said in late May — and it isn't just campaign rhetoric. According to an official with first-hand knowledge, she also made the point in a closed-door meeting with a top French military commander earlier this year. Le Pen also argued that France would eventually have to resume contact with Russia, added the official. “Today, it is … the pro-Russian faction that has regained power within the National Rally,” said a French lawmaker close to the government. Mélenchon has gone even further. A long-standing NATO critic , late last month he outlined some of his key international priorities, including fully withdrawing from NATO due to America's “openly hostile” stance. “There can be no question of remaining a member of NATO,” he told a conference in June. Advertisement Advertisement May Day Following through on that threat would have serious repercussions for NATO. “France is not merely a founding member but a key player in this alliance … not least because of its nuclear arsenal,” said Marie-Agnes Strack Zimmermann, chair of the European Parliament’s defense committee. “There is only one group that stands to gain from this — and that is the enemies of our freedom.” In theory, a decision to leave NATO’s command structures could take place immediately, explained French Lt. Gen. Michel Yakovleff, former vice-chief of staff at the alliance’s military headquarters. The French president does not need to consult parliament, and the one-year withdrawal clause in the NATO treaty only applies to countries leaving the alliance’s political structures — which wouldn't necessarily be the case under Le Pen's policy. Quitting NATO’s command structures would hurt France too. | Omar Havana/Getty Images In practice, however, it would likely take about one year, he estimated, as the transition would entail extracting around 1,000 officers permanently posted to NATO as well as setting up a liaison body to coordinate with the alliance going forward — just as De Gaulle did after France left the command. But even after De Gaulle's move, Paris continued to maintain close ties with NATO and frequently joined deployments. With a hard-line president next year, that could play out differently. The biggest fears in that scenario concern the future of the 1,200-strong French-led battlegroup in Romania, France's informal cooperation with NATO on nuclear arms and its specialized capabilities like satellites and intelligence, according to three NATO diplomats. Advertisement Advertisement For example, without France, NATO’s military planners would lose access to Europe's only nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, an amphibious fleet that includes Mistral-class vessels, CERES intelligence satellites and a powerful navy capable of deploying about 65 percent of its fleet — a rate even above the U.S., said Yakovleff. “The fact is we have a little of everything,” argued Yakovleff, adding that France's departure from the command structure would also have “budgetary consequences” for the alliance; France currently contributes 10 percent of NATO’s annual €5.3 billion operational budget . “It would weaken the alliance because we are still the most consequential power … after America,” he said. Friendly fire But quitting NATO’s command structures would hurt France too. While the country would keep its seat on NATO’s political bodies — including a say on triggering the alliance’s mutual defense clause — its powers would shrivel when it comes to military proposals, as many are pre-negotiated by NATO military staff, said Yakovleff. That means Paris could only “take or leave” final proposals. France would also lose high-level positions inside the alliance, said Yakovleff, including the post of Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, the deputy commander position at NATO’s air military headquarters and chief of staff at its Brunssum base in the Netherlands. And if France ends information-sharing, that could hamper its own access to information about what's happening in the rest of the alliance. Advertisement Leaving would “certainly [mean] losing influence” said Yakovleff. It “would cost a lot — politically, technically, operationally and structurally.” Politically, too, it could mean Germany becoming Europe's leading NATO member. “With France out and the Americans withdrawing … Germany would need to step up,” said the NATO diplomat cited above. “If you go out, you lose everything.” “There's already been this massive shift economically, politically, toward Germany and Poland, which are now the big spenders in GDP terms,” said Shea, the former NATO spokesperson. “It would simply accelerate what is happening already.” To prevent the worst-case scenario, Shea argued, NATO officials should start making behind-the-scenes overtures to lawmakers from the National Rally and France Unbowed to convince them of these downsides — and offer Paris more command posts to showcase its importance to the alliance. As the election gets closer, the prospect of a NATO-skeptic winning power in Paris is a growing worry inside the alliance. “We’ll survive,” said the same diplomat, but “it’s going to be very, very dangerous.” CORRECTION: This article has been updated to correct the location of Brunssum. It is in the Netherlands. Advertisement

https://www.odnako.org/el-mundo-russia-r.text: International El Mundo: “Russia ready for drone attacks from the sea in Italy, France and Spain” By John 2026-09-25 Add the Gazzetta del Sud as a source The map published by the Spanish newspaper EL MUNDO Russia is preparing for new drone attacks in Europe, but this time it will target Mediterranean countries: France, Spain and also Italy. The Spanish newspaper El Mundo writes this, according to which the US secret services have collected information on the Kremlin’s escalation plans and shared it with several European governments. «They will use drones launched from the sea, hidden in containers; it’s not difficult at all,” explains a source close to the Lithuanian Ministry of Defense. Lithuanian authorities know the type of drone the Russians could use against Spain, France or Italy. It would be a Gerbera: about two meters long, with a wingspan of 2.5 meters, weighing up to 18 kilograms, capable of reaching speeds of around 160 kilometers per hour and with a declared autonomy of 600 kilometers. A merchant ship can carry several of these drones, which are launched with much less difficulty than a Shahed or a Geran. From a distance of 200 or 300 kilometers from the coast, the flight would take about an hour and fifteen minutes or two hours, depending on the actual speed. Its small explosive load (4-5 kg) is not enough to destroy a large structure, but it can start a fire, damage exposed equipment or temporarily close a port or airport. All of Italy would be within range According to the map published by El Mundo, all of Italy – with the exception of the North-East – would be within range. Lithuania, like other countries, became aware of this information shortly after CIA director John Ratcliffe’s mysterious trip to Moscow on August 25. According to sources familiar with the alert, the governments of Spain, France and Italy were also informed that Russia was preparing a possible drone operation against one of these countries. Spain, France and Italy, writes El Mundo, “will have electoral campaigns and elections in 2027 and host radical forces capable of exploiting fear and disillusionment towards Ukraine. Especially in France and Italy, there are links or positions clearly aligned with the interests of the Kremlin.” The alert on drone attacks did not reach the Italian authorities According to qualified sources contacted by ANSA, the alleged alert reported by El Mundo regarding an imminent drone attack against Italy, France and Spain by the Russian Federation has not currently reached any operational, intelligence, diplomatic or military level. EU: “There is no specific alert but the news is not surprising” The European Commission has seen reports of a possible threat of Russian drone attacks against Italy, France and Spain and says it is “not a surprise”, but says it was not aware of the specific alert. «We know that our airspace is being tested and has been violated several times. We know that several hybrid attacks are underway targeting many of our member states”, declared spokesman Thomas Regnier, underlining that the issue “is a matter for national authorities”, but Brussels has “long experience of supporting states in case of need”. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Celebrations break out in Belgrade as Student List win elections by a landslide Serbia Serbian leader Aleksandar Vučić ousted by student movement in seismic election Vučić’s 12-year reign looks to have been ended by record turnout of voters in election provoked by student-led protests Ashifa Kassam , and Ana Milosavljević in Belgrade Sun 25 Oct 2026 19.42 EDT First published on Sun 25 Oct 2026 16.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The long-serving leader of Serbia , Aleksandar Vučić, has conceded defeat, ushering in a seismic political shift after a historic election that saw ​the increasingly authoritarian leader pitted against a student-led movement that had spent two years protesting against his government. Vučić pointed to preliminary results that suggested voters had overwhelmingly backed the students, potentially giving them a majority in the country’s 250-seat parliament. “We still do not have final ⁠results,” Vučić told supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade. “On the basis of a sample … it is clear ⁠that we have lost these ​elections, the Student ‌List has ‌won, they will have between 135 ‌and 140 seats and we will have 105.” View image in fullscreen Ilija Srdanović, first on the electoral list ‘Student List – Students Win’, celebrates after the first results of the parliamentary election in Belgrade. Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/Reuters A representative sample by the ​CeSID-IPSPS pollsters suggested that the ​Student List’s candidate list will have ​138 deputies, while Vučić’s rightwing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) garnered 104 seats. The remaining seats ‌were likely to be shared ​between ethnic ​national minority parties, said the pollsters. As news broke that Vučić’s 12 years in power had come to an end, celebrations erupted on the streets of Belgrade and other cities. In the capital, Ivana, 43, was ecstatic. “This feels like New Year’s Eve to me, like three New Year’s Eves all at once, really,” she said. “We can finally breathe again.” She added that she was hoping for swift accountability for top members of the ousted regime, a key campaign pledge from the Student List. View image in fullscreen A person celebrating the election results hugs a police officer as the result of the Serbian election prompts street celebrations in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Ana Milosavljevic/The Guardian Others offered handshakes, high fives and hugs to police officers in the streets, while a chorus of honking horns rang out from passing cars. At the headquarters of the Student List, supporters chanted “Victory, victory!” as they applauded, cried and traded hugs. “Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard,” said Radomir Saičić, a professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters. “Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future.” The scenes of joy came hours after a record number of voters turned up to cast their ballot on Sunday. Across the country, long lines snaked out of polling stations, with some reporting wait times of up to two hours. By 7pm local time pollsters and monitors CeSID and Ipsos put the turnout at 67.6%, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992. The high turnout, along with the estimated 150,000 people who flocked to the students’ final pre-election rally last week in Belgrade, fuelled early speculation that the students may have rallied enough support to launch a new political era in the Balkan country. Serbian voters around the world queue to cast ballots in snap parliamentary election In the lead-up to the vote, opinion polls had varied wildly, with analysts pointing to the high degree of uncertainty at play as the candidates representing the grassroots student movement went up against Vučić’s SNS. The results were watched across the world as part of 10 pivotal days of elections across the globe in which the authoritarian right is facing off against pro-democracy forces. The victory for the student-led movement in Serbia is also likely to reverberate across Europe, adding momentum to the youth and student protests that have rocked cities across the continent. View image in fullscreen A man, carrying his dog, leaves a polling station after casting his vote as people queue to vote during the parliamentary election in Belgrade. Photograph: Marko Đurica/Reuters As people waited for the election results to come in, speculation had begun to swirl online about whether Vučić would seek to hold on to power regardless. His swift admission of defeat, however, was reminiscent of his ally, Viktor Orbán , in neighbouring Hungary six months ago, fuelling hopes of a democratic resurgence to central Europe. The high-stakes election in the EU-candidate country traces back to November 2024, when a concrete canopy collapsed at the Novi Sad railway station, killing 16 people. The tragedy set off protests among students, snowballing into a broad anti-government movement as evidence suggested that slipshod construction, fraud and corruption were to blame for the roof collapse. As Vučić, the increasingly authoritarian leader who has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade, grappled with mounting pressure from the students, he resigned the presidency last month to gamble on snap elections. View image in fullscreen People in Belgrade celebrate Aleksandar Vučić’s defeat at the polls. Photograph: Armin Durgut/AP The students seized on the chance to transform the movement into political power. They announced a slate of 250 candidates for the 250-seat parliament, ranging from academics to athletes and farmers, as they called on voters to back their push to rebuild Serbia’s economy and restore its democracy. The campaign pitted them against the political monolith of Vučić’s SNS party, leaving them in an uphill battle against a ruling party that had taken over almost all of the broadcast channels and which wielded ministries and other state institutions as political tools. Vučić had repeatedly sought to undermine the students by accusing them of being stooges of foreign powers, a charge that the students have dismissed. As he pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, Vučić sought to present himself as a leader capable of walking the diplomatic tightrope between the country’s ties with the west, and Russia and China to steer Serbia through global uncertainties. Undaunted, the students took to the streets, staging rallies, turning up in the rural areas that had long been Vučić strongholds and going door-to-door as they sought to pitch themselves as the anti-establishment candidates and to rally voters behind their slogan of “Serbia or Mafia?” View image in fullscreen Former Serbian basketball player Dejan Bodiroga, a candidate for the Student List, celebrates after Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Petr David Josek/AP The message was reiterated on Sunday as Dejan Bodiroga, a candidate on the Student List and the Euroleague Basketball president, cast his ballot in Belgrade. “Today, above all, Serbia is fighting for freedom and for the return of a country that has been hijacked,” Bodiroga told reporters. “Serbia is voting today to decide which direction it will take – towards the future or the past.” In the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, both international and local election monitors expressed concerns about detentions and reports of surveillance and cyber-attacks against activists. On Sunday, independent monitoring groups warned of recorded cases of photographing of ballots that suggested pressure on voters, attempted vote-buying and carousel voting. Among them was Raša Nedeljkov of the election monitory CRTA, who said that “a large number of irregularities continue to be recorded, while violent incidents outside polling stations are also becoming increasingly frequent”.
